title: The Uffizi in two hours: a route through the rooms, and which ticket skips the line
subtitle: Start at the top, walk three corridors, come down one floor. What to stop for, and what each ticket is.
excerpt: A two-hour route through the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, stop by stop, from the three great Madonnas to Caravaggio, with the three lines at the door explained and what each kind of ticket includes.
secondary_keywords: what to see at the Uffizi
longtail_phrases: how to see the Uffizi in two hours
which Uffizi ticket skips the line

meta_title: The Uffizi in two hours: a route, and which ticket
meta_description: A two-hour route through the Uffizi: Giotto, Botticelli, the Tribuna, Leonardo, Caravaggio. The three lines at the door and what each ticket includes.

featured_image.alt: The long courtyard of the Uffizi in Florence seen from an upper floor, with the tower of Palazzo Vecchio at the far end

content_html:
[place attraction="uffizi-gallery-florence" city="florence"]

When Gian Gastone de' Medici died in 1737 without children, the family that had run Florence for three centuries came to an end. Tuscany passed to the house of Lorraine, and with it, by every custom of the time, the Medici collections: the paintings, the ancient statues, the jewels, the books. The courts of Europe expected to see them packed and carried off to Vienna.

His sister Anna Maria Luisa, the last of the line, signed an agreement with the new rulers that same year. They could have everything, on one condition: nothing was to leave Florence, so that it would remain an ornament of the state, of use to the public, and a reason for foreigners to come. She died in 1743. The Uffizi is what that clause protected, and it leaves you with a practical problem: there is far more here than one visit can hold. Two hours are enough for the heart of it, if you know the order.

How the building works

The Uffizi was not built as a museum. Giorgio Vasari began it in 1560 for Duke Cosimo I as offices, uffizi, for the magistrates of Florence. It is shaped like a long U: two wings running from Piazza della Signoria to the river, joined by a short one above the Arno.

The paintings are on two floors, and the visit starts at the top. You climb a wide staircase (there is a lift for those who need it), walk the three corridors of the upper floor, where the rooms open off in roughly the order in which the pictures were painted, then go down one level and work your way back to the exit. The route runs one way and going back against the flow is hard, so decide beforehand what you are stopping for.

A corridor of the top floor: windows on one side, ancient statues on the other, the rooms opening off it. Photo: Luca Aless, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The three lines at the door

Under the arcade of the courtyard there are three separate lines, each for a numbered door:

  • one for visitors without a reservation, which in season can last hours;
  • one where reservations and vouchers are exchanged for a paper ticket;
  • one for people holding a ticket for the current time slot.

Read your voucher to see which door it sends you to, and arrive a quarter of an hour early. Everybody goes through the security check, so no ticket skips that. Large bags and umbrellas go to the cloakroom.

The route, stop by stop

1. Three Madonnas

The first large room holds three enthroned Madonnas on gold, by Cimabue, Duccio and Giotto, painted within a few decades of each other around 1300. Look at Giotto's last: under the cloth there is a body with weight. Much of what follows in the building starts here.

2. The Duke and Duchess of Urbino

Piero della Francesca painted Federico da Montefeltro and his wife Battista Sforza facing each other in profile. The duke had lost his right eye and the bridge of his nose in a tournament, which is why he shows his left side.

3. Botticelli

The busiest rooms of the gallery. The Primavera, of about 1480, is painted on wood. The Birth of Venus, a few years later, is on canvas, which was unusual in Florence then. Stand to one side and wait: the groups move on every few minutes.

The Birth of Venus on the far wall of its room. It is rarely this empty. Photo: Fabrizio Garrisi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

4. The Tribuna

An eight-sided room finished in 1584 by Bernardo Buontalenti for Francesco I, to hold the most precious things the Medici owned. The dome is set with thousands of pieces of mother-of-pearl. You do not walk in: you look from the doorways.

The Tribuna, built in the 1580s for the best pieces of the Medici. You look in from the doorways. Photo: Armin Kleiner, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

5. The corridor on the river

The short side of the U is the place to pause. On one side the windows look down the courtyard, on the other over the Arno and the Ponte Vecchio, with the roof of the Vasari Corridor running along the top of the bridge.

The Ponte Vecchio from a window of the short corridor on the river. Photo: Yair Haklai, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

6. Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael

In the third corridor: Leonardo's Annunciation, painted when he was in his early twenties, and his unfinished Adoration of the Magi. Then Michelangelo's round Holy Family, the Doni Tondo, the only finished panel painting that is certainly his, and Raphael's Madonna of the Goldfinch.

7. Down one floor: Titian and Caravaggio

The first floor is where tired visitors speed up, and they miss Titian's Venus of Urbino of 1538, Caravaggio's Medusa, painted on a round parade shield, his young Bacchus, and Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith Beheading Holofernes. From here the signs to the exit take another ten minutes of walking.

If you have time left, the terrace café at the end of the upper floor sits above the Loggia dei Lanzi, level with the tower of Palazzo Vecchio.

What the tickets include

  • A priority or reserved entrance ticket is entry at a fixed time and nothing else. It spares you the first line, not the security check.
  • A hosted entry ticket adds a person who meets you outside and gets you to the right door. That person is not a guide.
  • A ticket with an audio tour adds commentary in the partner's app on your own phone, with directions from room to room. Bring earphones.
  • An audio tour "without a ticket" is the commentary alone. You still need to book your entry.
  • Combined tickets pair the Uffizi with the Accademia, or with the Pitti Palace and the Boboli Gardens, which are across the river. Check how many days you have to use each part.

The Vasari Corridor, the raised passage from the Uffizi over the Ponte Vecchio, reopened to visitors at the end of 2024. It is sold as an addition to an Uffizi ticket, with a time slot of its own, and an ordinary ticket does not include it.

These are the Uffizi tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner q="uffizi" match="uffizi" limit="6"]

When to go

The Uffizi is closed on Mondays, which makes Tuesday the heaviest day of the week. The first slot of the morning and the last two hours of the afternoon are the calmest. On the first Sunday of the month state museums in Italy are free, and the line shows it. Hours and evening openings change through the year: the current ones are on our page for the Uffizi Gallery.

From here

You come out a few steps from Piazza della Signoria, with Palazzo Vecchio and the statues of the Loggia dei Lanzi, all free to look at. The Ponte Vecchio is two minutes along the river. Michelangelo's David is a quarter of an hour north on foot, in the Accademia. For the rest of Florence, or to fit it into a longer trip, open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Verum3414, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you see the Uffizi in two hours?
faqs.a: You can see its best-known works in two hours if you follow the one-way route with a short list: the three Madonnas, Piero della Francesca, Botticelli, the Tribuna, Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, then Titian and Caravaggio on the floor below.

faqs.q: Which Uffizi ticket skips the line?
faqs.a: Any ticket reserved for a time slot avoids the line for visitors without a reservation, which is the long one. Nobody skips the security check, and a voucher often has to be exchanged for a paper ticket at a separate door first.

faqs.q: Where is the Birth of Venus in the Uffizi?
faqs.a: On the upper floor, in the Botticelli rooms along the first corridor, near the Primavera. The visit starts on that floor, so you reach it in the first half hour.

faqs.q: Is the Vasari Corridor included in the Uffizi ticket?
faqs.a: No. The corridor reopened at the end of 2024 and is sold as an addition to an Uffizi ticket, with its own time slot. An ordinary ticket does not include it.

faqs.q: Which day is the Uffizi closed?
faqs.a: The Uffizi is closed on Mondays. Hours and special openings change during the year, so check the current ones before your visit.

title: Seeing Michelangelo's David without the queue: how the Accademia in Florence works
subtitle: A small museum on a narrow street, two lines on the pavement, and one statue everybody came for.
excerpt: How to see Michelangelo's David at the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence without losing a morning: the two lines, how a reserved slot works, what else is inside, and what the partner's tickets include.
longtail_phrases: how to see the David in Florence without queuing
how long does the Accademia Gallery take
is the David in Piazza della Signoria the real one
do you need to book the Accademia in advance
what else is in the Accademia besides David
meta_title: See Michelangelo's David without the queue: Accademia
meta_description: The two lines at the Accademia in Florence, how a reserved slot works, what is inside besides the David, and what each ticket includes.

featured_image.alt: Michelangelo's David in its domed tribune at the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence

content_html:
[place attraction="galleria-dell-accademia" city="florence"]

The block of marble had been lying in the yard of Florence Cathedral for nearly forty years. Two sculptors had started on it and given up. It was very tall, awkwardly shallow, and the stone was not of the best. In the summer of 1501 the cathedral's works office handed it to Michelangelo, who was twenty-six, and he finished the figure early in 1504.

The statue had been ordered for a buttress high on the cathedral. Once people saw it, a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci and Botticelli met to decide on a better place, and the David was set up beside the door of the town hall, in the open air. It stood there for 369 years. In 1873 it was rolled through the streets on rails, inside a wooden frame, to the Accademia, and the domed room built to receive it opened in 1882. Nearly everyone who enters this museum comes for that one figure, which is why the difficulty of the visit is on the pavement outside.

Why the line is so long

The Accademia is a small museum on a narrow street, Via Ricasoli, with no forecourt and a limit on how many people may be inside at once. So the waiting happens on the pavement, in two lines:

  • one for visitors with a reservation, grouped by time slot;
  • one for visitors without, who are let in only as space allows. In the warm months that can mean hours, in the sun.

Everybody passes a security check at the door.

How a reserved slot works

A reservation is for a short entry window at a fixed time. In most cases what you receive is a voucher, which has to be exchanged for a paper ticket before you join the line: at a ticket desk near the entrance, or at a meeting point named by the seller. Allow fifteen to twenty minutes for that.

"Skip the line" here means the reserved line instead of the other one. It is shorter, not absent, and it moves at the speed of the security check.

The museum is closed on Mondays. The first slots of the morning and the last hour and a half of the day are the quietest. On the first Sunday of the month entry is free, and the pavement is at its worst.

What you see, in order

The whole museum takes forty-five minutes to an hour, and the rooms prepare you for the statue if you let them.

The Hall of the Colossus

In the middle of the first room stands Giambologna's full-size plaster model for the Abduction of a Sabine Woman. The marble made from it is in the Loggia dei Lanzi, in Piazza della Signoria. Around the walls are Florentine paintings of the years when Michelangelo was a boy.

The first hall, with Giambologna's plaster model in the middle. Photo: Francesco Bini, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Hall of the Prisoners

A long gallery leads to the David, lined with four unfinished figures that Michelangelo began for the tomb of Pope Julius II, and with his St Matthew. Each seems to be pulling itself out of the block. Go slowly here: the chisel marks show how he worked, from the front of the stone inwards.

One of the unfinished Prisoners, with the David at the end of the hall. Photo: Petra 99MI, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Tribune

The David stands under a skylight, a little over five metres high with its base. Walk all the way round. From behind you see the sling lying across the shoulder and the tree stump that braces the right leg. The head and the right hand are large for the body, perhaps because the figure was planned to be seen from far below.

It has been hurt twice. In 1527, during a riot, a bench thrown from a window of the town hall broke the left arm into three pieces. In 1991 a man struck the toes of the left foot with a hammer. That is why there is a barrier.

What most people skip

Beyond the Tribune a long hall is filled with the white plaster casts of the nineteenth-century sculptor Lorenzo Bartolini. A side wing holds the Medici collection of musical instruments, with pieces by Stradivari and by Bartolomeo Cristofori, who invented the piano in Florence. Upstairs are paintings on gold ground.

The hall of plaster casts, beyond the David, where most visitors do not go. Photo: Andy Montgomery, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

What the partner's listings include

  • A priority entry ticket with an audio tour and a city walk includes entry, commentary for the gallery in the partner's app, and a walk through the centre afterwards. The voucher is exchanged for a paper ticket at a meeting point.
  • A gallery ticket with a sightseeing audio tour includes entry and an audio walk through the city. Read the exclusions: on this one the commentary does not cover the inside of the gallery.
  • An audio tour "without a ticket" is commentary only. You book your entry yourself.
  • A combined Accademia and Uffizi ticket covers both museums, with an audio tour.
  • The other listings are audio walks on the theme of Michelangelo. They pass the door, they do not go in.

These are the Accademia tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="galleria-dell-accademia" match="accademia" limit="6"]

If the slots are gone: the two copies

Florence has two full-size copies outdoors, both free. The marble one has stood since 1910 on the spot the original occupied, at the door of Palazzo Vecchio. A bronze one looks over the city from Piazzale Michelangelo, on the hill across the river.

They give you the size and the setting. They do not give you the surface, and the copy in the square is seen against a busy wall instead of an empty niche. If the David is the reason you came to Florence, book the original.

The copy at the door of Palazzo Vecchio, where the original stood until 1873. Photo: Peter K Burian, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Hours change through the year: see our page for the Galleria dell'Accademia.

From here

The convent of San Marco, with the frescoes Fra Angelico painted in the monks' cells, is two minutes north. The cathedral is five minutes south, straight down Via Ricasoli. The Medici Chapels, with more Michelangelo, are ten minutes west, and the Uffizi a quarter of an hour away. See what else there is in Florence, or open the attractions map of Italy.

Cover photo: Jörg Bittner Unna, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: How can you see Michelangelo's David without queuing?
faqs.a: Reserve a time slot in advance. You then use the reserved line, which is much shorter than the line for visitors without a booking, though everyone still passes the security check.

faqs.q: Do you need to book the Accademia in advance?
faqs.a: It is not compulsory, but without a reservation you wait in a separate line that is admitted only as space allows, which can take hours in season. Popular slots sell out days ahead.

faqs.q: Is the David in Piazza della Signoria the real one?
faqs.a: No. It is a marble copy placed there in 1910, on the spot where the original stood from 1504 to 1873. The original is in the Galleria dell'Accademia.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Accademia take?
faqs.a: Forty-five minutes to an hour for the whole museum. Add fifteen to twenty minutes before your slot if your voucher has to be exchanged for a ticket.

faqs.q: What else is in the Accademia besides the David?
faqs.a: Michelangelo's four unfinished Prisoners and his St Matthew, Giambologna's plaster model for the Sabine group, a hall of nineteenth-century plaster casts, Florentine paintings and a collection of historic musical instruments.

title: Pompeii in a day from Naples or Rome: how to get there, and what to see in three hours
subtitle: A whole town, three entrances, one commuter train. A route from the Forum to the amphitheatre that never doubles back.
excerpt: How to reach Pompeii from Naples and from Rome, which entrance to use, how the named tickets work, and a three-hour route through the ancient town from Porta Marina to the amphitheatre.
secondary_keywords: Pompeii from Rome in a day
what to see in Pompeii in three hours
longtail_phrases: how to get to Pompeii from Naples by train
can you visit Pompeii from Rome in a day
what to see in Pompeii in three hours
which entrance to use at Pompeii
how long do you need at Pompeii
meta_title: Pompeii in a day from Naples or Rome: three-hour route
meta_description: The train from Naples, the long day from Rome, which entrance to use, how the tickets work, and a three-hour route through Pompeii.

featured_image.alt: Columns of the Forum of Pompeii with Mount Vesuvius on the horizon

content_html:
[place attraction="pompeii" city="pompei"]

In the 1590s the architect Domenico Fontana dug a canal to carry the water of the river Sarno to the mills of Torre Annunziata. Part of it was a tunnel through a low hill that local people called La Civita, the city. His workmen cut through painted walls and carved inscriptions, and carried on. Nobody asked what was under the hill.

Digging began only in 1748, on the orders of the Bourbon king of Naples, who wanted statues for his collection. It took until 1763 for an inscription to turn up that named the place: Pompeii, buried under several metres of ash and pumice in AD 79. What has been uncovered since is not a monument but a town, about 66 hectares inside its walls, two thirds of it excavated. That is the difficulty of a day trip: getting there is simple, and the place is too big to wander.

From Naples

Take the Circumvesuviana, the commuter railway to Sorrento. It leaves from Napoli Porta Nolana and stops a few minutes later at Napoli Piazza Garibaldi, on the lower level of the central station. Get off at Pompei Scavi-Villa dei Misteri, a little over half an hour away. The main entrance to the ruins, Porta Marina, is across the road.

The trains are frequent, plain and often packed, with no reserved seats. Keep a hand on your bag. Do not get off at a station called simply Pompei: those, on another branch and on the national railway, are in the modern town, a ten to fifteen minute walk from the entrance at the other end of the site.

From Rome

It can be done in a day, and it is a long one. A high-speed train from Roma Termini reaches Napoli Centrale in a little over an hour. From there you go downstairs to the Circumvesuviana, as above. Count on two and a half hours from door to gate, each way. Leave Rome by eight, and book a return with some margin, because the local line is not punctual.

The other way is a coach that leaves Rome in the morning with entry included. The road takes about three hours each way, which leaves two to three hours among the ruins. Read whether a guide is part of it: on several such trips the visit itself is on your own.

Tickets and entrances

There are three entrances. Porta Marina, beside the station, is the busiest. Piazza Esedra, a few minutes downhill, is where many groups go in. Piazza Anfiteatro, at the eastern end, is the quiet one.

Since November 2024 the park admits no more than 20,000 people a day and issues tickets in the visitor's name, so carry an identity document. In the busy months tickets are tied to a morning or an afternoon entry. The park has also been selling two levels of ticket: one for the town inside the walls, and a fuller one that adds the villas outside them, among them the Villa of the Mysteries. Check which one you are buying.

Three hours, from Porta Marina to the amphitheatre

Walk the town from west to east and leave by Piazza Anfiteatro. Houses open and close in rotation, so do not build the day around a single one.

  • The Forum. The main square, with the Temple of Jupiter at its head and Vesuvius directly behind. Before the eruption the mountain was green with vineyards, and nobody in the town knew what it was. Along one side, behind bars, are shelves of jars and several casts of victims.
  • The Forum Baths and the House of the Tragic Poet. Just north of the square. At the door of the house is the mosaic of a chained dog with the words cave canem, beware of the dog.
  • The House of the Faun. The largest house in Pompeii, a whole block. The small bronze dancing faun in its pool is a copy, and the great mosaic of Alexander in battle was lifted from a floor here. The originals are in Naples.
  • Via dell'Abbondanza. The main street: stepping stones for crossing, ruts worn by cart wheels, the counters of food bars with jars sunk into them, and election slogans painted on the walls. The Stabian Baths and the brothel, which always has a line, are just off it.
  • The theatres. A large open one for about five thousand people and a small covered one beside it.
  • The Garden of the Fugitives. Thirteen people who died trying to leave, lying where they fell. The casts were made by a method devised in 1863 by Giuseppe Fiorelli, who poured plaster into the hollows that bodies had left in the hardened ash.
  • The amphitheatre. Built about 70 BC, the oldest stone amphitheatre still standing. In AD 59 a riot here between Pompeians and visitors from Nuceria was so bloody that Rome banned games in the town for ten years.

Via dell'Abbondanza, the main street, with its stepping stones. Photo: Adam Harangozó, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Garden of the Fugitives, at the quiet end of the town, with the mountain behind it. Photo: Miguel Hermoso Cuesta, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The amphitheatre, built about 70 BC, at the far end of the route. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A ticket with an audio tour includes entry and a route narrated in the partner's app, on your own phone.
  • The audio tour alone has no entry ticket. You buy that separately.
  • MAP, Magic Ancient Pompeii, is not the ruins. It is a separate indoor attraction near Porta Marina that shows the town reconstructed in 3D.
  • Day trips from Rome bundle the coach and the entry. Check the time on site and whether anyone guides you.
  • Combinations with Herculaneum and Vesuvius, or with the Amalfi Coast, are full days in which Pompeii gets the smaller share.

These are the Pompeii tickets, audio tours and day trips our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner q="pompeii" match="pompei" limit="6"]

On the ground

  • There is almost no shade. Bring a hat and water; there are drinking fountains inside.
  • The streets are paved with large uneven blocks. Wear closed shoes with a firm sole. Pushchairs struggle.
  • Large bags and suitcases are not let in. There is left luggage at the entrances.

The paving you walk on for three hours: large, uneven and polished. Photo: Gary Todd, via Wikimedia Commons.

Hours shorten in winter. The current ones are on our page for Pompeii.

From here

The objects found in the houses, with the Alexander mosaic among them, are in the National Archaeological Museum in Naples, which makes the best second half of the day. Herculaneum, smaller and better preserved, is on the same railway line. See what else there is around Pompei and in Naples, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Commonists, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to Pompeii from Naples?
faqs.a: Take the Circumvesuviana train towards Sorrento from Napoli Porta Nolana or Napoli Piazza Garibaldi and get off at Pompei Scavi-Villa dei Misteri, a little over half an hour away. The Porta Marina entrance is across the road.

faqs.q: Can you visit Pompeii from Rome in a day?
faqs.a: Yes, as a long day. A high-speed train to Naples takes a little over an hour, then the local train a little over half an hour: about two and a half hours each way door to gate. Coach day trips with entry are the alternative.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Pompeii?
faqs.a: Three hours cover the main sights on a route from the Forum to the amphitheatre. The town is large enough to fill a whole day if you add the villas outside the walls.

faqs.q: Which entrance to Pompeii is best?
faqs.a: Porta Marina is beside the Pompei Scavi station and close to the Forum, so it suits a west to east route. Piazza Anfiteatro, at the other end, is quieter and makes a good exit.

faqs.q: Do you need to book Pompeii tickets in advance?
faqs.a: In the busy months it is wise. The park limits the number of visitors each day and issues tickets in the visitor's name, so bring an identity document.

title: Climbing the Leaning Tower of Pisa: who can go up, and how the timed ticket works
subtitle: About 250 worn steps, a fixed slot, no bags and no small children. What to know before you book.
excerpt: You can climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa, at a fixed time and with rules: who is not admitted, how the slot and the cloakroom work, what the ticket also covers, and whether the climb is worth it.
focus_keyword: climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa
secondary_keywords: Leaning Tower of Pisa timed entry
longtail_phrases: can you climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa
how many steps in the Leaning Tower of Pisa
can children climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa
how does the timed ticket for the Tower of Pisa work

meta_title: Climbing the Leaning Tower of Pisa: timed ticket, rules
meta_description: Yes, you can climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Who is not admitted, how the timed slot and the cloakroom work, and what the ticket also covers.

featured_image.alt: The Leaning Tower of Pisa and the cathedral on the lawn of the Piazza dei Miracoli

content_html:
[place attraction="leaning-tower-of-pisa" city="pisa"]

Work on the bell tower of Pisa Cathedral began in August 1173. Five years later, when the builders had reached the third storey, the ground on the south side started to give way: the tower stands on soft clay and sand, on foundations only about three metres deep. Then Pisa went to war, and the site lay idle for almost a century. That pause is thought to have saved the building, because it gave the soil time to settle under the weight.

When work resumed in 1272, the masons made the new storeys slightly taller on the low side to bring the line back, which is why the tower is faintly curved. The bell chamber was added in 1372, and the lean kept growing. On 7 January 1990 the tower was closed. Engineers hung some six hundred tonnes of lead on its high side, then drew out soil from beneath it, a little at a time, until the top had come back by about 45 centimetres. It reopened in December 2001, leaning roughly four degrees, and since then visitors have been allowed up again.

Can you climb it?

Yes. Visitors go up at fixed times, in groups, watched by staff, and the whole visit lasts about half an hour.

The staircase winds between the inner and the outer wall of the cylinder: about 250 steps, with no lift. The marble treads are worn into hollows, and because the tower tilts, the hollows move from one side of the step to the other as you turn. You feel yourself pushed against the outer wall, then the inner one. Near the top the stair comes out on an open gallery, and a last narrow flight leads to the bell chamber, where seven bells hang in the arches.

The top of the tower: the last open gallery and, set back above it, the bell chamber. Photo: FaceMePLS, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The bells in the arches of the top level. Photo: Luca Aless, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Who is not admitted

  • Children under eight. This is a rule of the tower, not advice, and there are no exceptions for children carried in arms.
  • Anyone under eighteen without an adult.
  • The climb is also a poor idea for anyone with a heart condition, vertigo or trouble with stairs. The steps are slippery when wet.

How the timed ticket works

  • The slot is exact. Your ticket carries a time, and the places in each slot are limited. In season the good hours sell out days ahead.
  • Late means lost. Be at the foot of the tower ten to fifteen minutes before. If you miss the group, the ticket is not moved to a later one.
  • No bags, of any size. Handbags included. They go to the free cloakroom on the square before you line up, and it takes them only shortly before your slot. You go up with a phone or a camera in your hand.
  • The cathedral comes with it. A tower ticket also covers the cathedral next door, which has no fixed time: go in before or after, on the same day.
  • The rest is separate. The Baptistery, the Camposanto and the two museums of the square are on their own tickets or combined ones, without a time slot.

The nave of the cathedral, which a tower ticket also opens. Photo: Eric Kilby, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Is the climb worth it?

The square is free, and the tower from outside is the main sight: you do not need a ticket to see it lean. What the climb adds is the odd feeling of the tilt under your feet, and a view straight down onto the roof of the cathedral, then over the red roofs of the town to the hills.

The famous story belongs to the top, too: Galileo, born in Pisa, is said to have dropped two weights from here to show that they fall together. It comes from a biography written by his pupil long afterwards, and there is no record that it happened.

If you are travelling with small children, or the slots are gone, put the time into the Baptistery, the largest in Italy, whose dome has a long echo that the guards show off at intervals, and into the quiet cloister of the Camposanto.

Looking down from the tower: the edge of the square, and the roofs of Pisa. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A tower ticket, sold as general admission or as a fast track ticket for the tower and the cathedral, is a timed entry to the tower with entry to the cathedral. One of them has you collect the tickets at a desk on the square first, so arrive early.
  • A listing called "Museum ticket and audio tour" names a museum in its title, while its list of inclusions mentions a ticket to the tower. Open it and read what is written before you pay.
  • The "Leaning Tower Legends" audio tour is commentary only, with no entry.
  • The audio walk through Pisa covers the city and the square from outside. No tickets are part of it.

Getting there

From Florence a regional train reaches Pisa Centrale in about an hour. From that station the square is twenty-five minutes on foot, across the Arno and through the old town, or a short bus ride. Some trains also stop at Pisa San Rossore, a small station ten minutes' walk from the tower.

On a day trip, leave at least an hour between the arrival of your train and your slot. Hours and last entries change with the season: see our page for the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

From here

The cathedral, older than the tower by a century, is the building the tower was made to serve. Ten minutes away is Piazza dei Cavalieri, the square Vasari redesigned for the Medici, and beyond it the river, lined with painted palaces. Lucca, inside its ring of walls, is half an hour by train. See what else there is in Pisa, or open the attractions map of Italy.

Cover photo: PaestumPaestum, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors go up in groups at fixed times, with a ticket for an exact slot. The visit lasts about half an hour and there is no lift.

faqs.q: How many steps are there in the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
faqs.a: About 250, on a spiral staircase between the inner and outer walls. The marble is worn and the tilt makes the climb feel uneven.

faqs.q: Can children climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
faqs.a: Children under eight are not admitted, even carried. Anyone under eighteen has to go up with an adult.

faqs.q: Can you take a bag up the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
faqs.a: No. Bags of any size, handbags included, must be left in the free cloakroom on the square before your slot. You can carry a phone or a camera.

faqs.q: Does the tower ticket include Pisa Cathedral?
faqs.a: Yes, a tower ticket also covers the cathedral, which has no fixed time on the same day. The Baptistery, the Camposanto and the museums need their own or a combined ticket.

title: Pinacoteca di Brera in Milan: is it worth it, and what to see in ninety minutes
subtitle: Milan's great painting gallery is one floor, one loop, and seven pictures you should not walk past.

featured_image.alt: The two-storey arcaded courtyard of the Brera palace in Milan, with a bronze statue at its centre

content_html:
[place attraction="pinacoteca-di-brera" city="milan"]

In the middle of the courtyard of the Brera palace stands a bronze Napoleon, naked, larger than life, holding a small winged Victory in one hand. It was cast from a model by Antonio Canova, who showed the emperor as Mars the Peacemaker. He is there because the gallery upstairs is his doing.

Under French rule, churches and convents all over northern Italy were closed, and their paintings were sent to Milan, the capital of Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy, to make a national gallery on the model of the Louvre. It opened on 15 August 1809, the emperor's birthday. Two centuries later most visitors to Milan spend their effort on a slot for the Last Supper and on the roof of the cathedral, and wonder whether a painting gallery deserves an hour and a half of a short stay.

Is it worth it?

If you like Italian painting at all, yes. The reason is the way the collection was formed. This was not a prince's cabinet of small pictures chosen to please. It is made of altarpieces, many of them enormous, taken from chapels in Venice, Lombardy, Emilia and the Marche, and several are works you have seen in books all your life.

It is also an easy museum. The rooms are on one floor and form a single loop, so you cannot get lost, and ninety minutes are enough. It is rarely crowded the way the Uffizi is, and tickets can usually be had at short notice, which cannot be said of the Last Supper.

Skip it if what you want from Milan is design, fashion or modern art, or if you are travelling with small children who have already done one museum that day.

The building is half the visit

The palace was a Jesuit college, begun in the seventeenth century. When the order was suppressed in 1773, Empress Maria Theresa of Austria turned it into a house of learning: an academy of fine arts, founded in 1776, a library, an observatory and a botanical garden. All four are still here. Art students cross the courtyard with portfolios, and the gallery is up the double staircase, on the first floor.

The courtyard is free to enter. So is the small botanical garden behind the palace, when it is open.

What to see, in order

  • Mantegna, the Lamentation over the Dead Christ. A body seen from the soles of the feet, shortened so sharply that it seems to slide towards you. It is a small picture, and it was still in the painter's studio when he died in 1506.
  • Giovanni Bellini, the Pietà. Mother and son, cheek to cheek, against a cold sky.
  • Gentile and Giovanni Bellini, St Mark Preaching in Alexandria. One of the largest pictures in the building, made for a confraternity in Venice. Gentile began it, and his brother finished it after Gentile's death in 1507.
  • Piero della Francesca, the Montefeltro Altarpiece. Federico da Montefeltro kneels in armour before the Virgin, in profile as always. Above her head an egg hangs from a shell on a thread.
  • Raphael, the Marriage of the Virgin. Signed and dated 1504 on the temple in the background, when he was twenty-one.
  • Caravaggio, the Supper at Emmaus. Painted in 1606, in the months after he killed a man in Rome and fled. It is far darker and quieter than his earlier version in London.
  • Hayez, The Kiss. Painted in 1859, the year Lombardy was freed from Austrian rule, and read ever since as a picture of the new Italy. It hangs near the end of the loop.

Mantegna's Dead Christ, seen from the feet. Photo: reproduction of a painting in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

St Mark Preaching in Alexandria, by the Bellini brothers, with visitors for scale. Photo: SunOfErat, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The centre of Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin, painted in 1504. Photo: Miguel Hermoso Cuesta, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Kiss, by Francesco Hayez, 1859. Photo: Miguel Hermoso Cuesta, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

On the way you pass a restoration workshop with glass walls, where conservators work in view of the public.

What the ticket covers now

A ticket to the Pinacoteca covers the gallery in the Brera palace, usually for a reserved time. In December 2024 a second building opened a short walk away: Palazzo Citterio, which now shows the gallery's twentieth-century collections. It has been sold with a combined ticket, so if modern art matters to you, check whether yours includes it. Older descriptions of the Brera, and some listings, still mention modern works among its highlights.

The gallery is closed on Mondays.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A Pinacoteca di Brera ticket is entry to the gallery and nothing more. The list above is all you need to go with it.
  • A ticket with an audio tour adds about an hour of commentary in the partner's app, with directions from room to room. Bring earphones.
  • A ticket and audio tour with a walk through the Brera quarter adds an audio walk around the streets outside.
  • Listings called only "audio tour", of the gallery, of the gallery and the quarter, or of the district alone, do not include entry. You buy your ticket separately.

These are the Brera tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="pinacoteca-di-brera" match="pinacoteca" limit="6"]

Practical notes

  • The nearest metro stations are Lanza, on line M2, and Montenapoleone, on line M3, each a few minutes on foot.
  • Bags and umbrellas go into lockers at the entrance.
  • The first hour of the day and late afternoon are the quietest.

Hours and special openings are on our page for the Pinacoteca di Brera.

From here

The streets around the palace, Via Brera and Via Fiori Chiari, are the old artists' quarter, now full of galleries and restaurant tables. Sforza Castle is ten minutes to the west, with its free courtyards and the park behind it. La Scala is five minutes south, and Milan Cathedral a quarter of an hour. For the rest of Milan, or a route through the north, open the trip planner for Italy.

faqs.q: Is the Pinacoteca di Brera worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like Italian painting. It holds Mantegna, Bellini, Piero della Francesca, Raphael, Caravaggio and Hayez on one floor, it is easy to walk in ninety minutes, and it is rarely as crowded as the better-known sights of Milan.

faqs.q: How long does the Pinacoteca di Brera take?
faqs.a: About ninety minutes for the main rooms at a steady pace. The gallery is a single loop on one floor.

faqs.q: What are the most famous paintings in the Brera?
faqs.a: Mantegna's Lamentation over the Dead Christ, Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin, Piero della Francesca's Montefeltro Altarpiece, Caravaggio's Supper at Emmaus and The Kiss by Francesco Hayez.

faqs.q: Does the Brera ticket include Palazzo Citterio?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Palazzo Citterio, which opened in December 2024 with the gallery's twentieth-century collections, has been sold with a combined ticket. Check what yours covers.

faqs.q: Which day is the Pinacoteca di Brera closed?
faqs.a: It is closed on Mondays. Hours and special openings change, so check the current ones before you go.
